title: The quick-watch shelf
prompt: The app's quick-watch shelf shows the five shortest films. Write `solve(movies)` so it returns them as `movie_id`, `title` and `runtime_min`, shortest first.
rules: Sort by `runtime_min`, shortest first. Films with the same runtime are sorted by `title` from A to Z, then by `movie_id`.
A film with no runtime goes after every film that has one.
The table may hold the same film row twice: each film takes only one place on the shelf.
Return at most five rows, with three columns in this order: `movie_id`, `title`, `runtime_min`.
hints: Remove repeated rows first with `distinct()`, then sort, then keep five rows with `limit(5)`.
An ascending sort puts missing values first. `F.col("runtime_min").asc_nulls_last()` moves them to the end.
List all three sort keys in one `orderBy`, so ties at the fifth place are settled the same way every time.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(movies):
    # Return the five shortest films, shortest first.
    return movies
explanation: Three steps, in this order: `distinct()` so a film delivered twice can't take two places, `orderBy(F.col("runtime_min").asc_nulls_last(), "title", "movie_id")` so the shortest come first and every tie is settled, then `limit(5)`. A plain ascending sort puts films with no runtime first, which would fill the shelf with unknowns; `asc_nulls_last()` sends them to the end. `limit` must come after the sort: `limit` first keeps five rows from wherever they happen to be and only then sorts them. `select` can go before or after, and `dropDuplicates()` works like `distinct()`.
